cards.title: U.S. workers took home their smallest share of capital since at least 1947

depth.text: workers are getting a **smaller slice** of the economy while **corporate profits** keep climbing

The Bureau of Labor Statistics says labor’s share of economic output fell to **52.8%** in the second quarter of 2026, down from 53.6% the quarter before and the lowest since records began in 1947. The article points to **automation** as one possible pressure, but says **AI job displacement** has not yet shown up meaningfully in economic data.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters call the shift an unhealthy trend; others point to demographics and tooling costs, or question whether the share measure proves workers are personally worse off.

comments.text: This shouldn't be a surprise. The US came out of WWII with similarly high debt to GDP. They only corrected that through financial repression, and that's likely to be their only chance of lowering that debt ratio today. If we don't spend the next few decades skating by while the currency is debased under our noses, I assume its because there's a much more severe and tragic response.

Sounds like the policies that were put in place are doing what they were designed to do, and directing money to where they were intended to. The work on technology to take the place of policy is proceeding, thought slower than the leadership would prefer.

Machine intelligence could drive as much transfer from labor to capital in the next decade as the previous wage-to-financial economy produced in forty years. This will push wealth concentration in leading OECD economies beyond the inequality seen in Brazil and Mexico.

Also productivity costs more in tooling than ever before per worker, so it's not a surprise that a smaller amount of capital goes to humans when the gains are majority from capital outlays, not labor improvements. Here's BLS data for total cost to employ for the last 25 years. https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/ECIALLCIV Note how much it has increased over simply wages, as it costs more and more…

So here's what I don't get: The United States is the world's largest consumer market. From what I can find, personal consumption expenditures (PCE) account for about two-thirds to 70% of total US economic output. We live and die on consumer spending and confidence. So next we automate the bejeebus out of this economy with AI robots and Elon believes it grows 3x in under five years. Splendid. But…

cards.title: Postgres 19 is late because so many more bugs are being found now

depth.text: the Postgres release is running late as **AI** helps people find **more bugs**

One commenter says AI-assisted hunting turned up **hundreds of bug candidates**, including serialization anomalies, foreign-key issues and **planner bugs**. Others say bug fixing may take time from feature work but can **harden the codebase**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say LLMs are surfacing old bugs and the delay is a worthwhile quality push; others question whether the reports are reliable or AI-generated contributions are lowering code quality.

comments.text: Ok, but does (s)he know? It's just guessing, so unfounded non-news? "It’s possible that some of this jump is the result of committers making more mistakes this year than they did last year, but I don’t think anyone who works on the project really believes that’s the main cause. Rather, it seems likely that PostgreSQL committers were about as conservative in 2026 as they were in preceding years…

> This year is going to be different. PostgreSQL 19 most likely won’t be released until November… […] So, what happened? The short answer is that LLMs happened. I did a little AI-assisted bug-hunting in Postgres this summer in between jobs, and the haul was staggering. Multiple serialization anomalies (eg [0] [1] [2]), foreign key integrity issues ([3] [4]), planner correctness bugs such as [5]. Various CVE-worthy vulnerabilities. An unfixable timezone bug [6]. The process should now be: write your specs in lean, LLMs fill the gaps, then you translate the proof into your end product software. Otherwise LLMs will simply keep finding bugs, both in old and new code.

I feel like AI is amazing for read only “search” tasks (query this, look for bugs, find vulnerabilities) but it’s not quite as good for “write” tasks like “add this feature”. Search tasks are easily verified, code changes are much harder to verify

cards.title: Show HN: OmniDiff – Opensource, super fast, content aware Git difftool, in Rust

depth.text: someone built **OmniDiff**, a Git diff tool that can compare **code, images, PDFs, and more**

The author looked at 7,400 repositories listed in Gentoo packages, sampled **2,000 diffs**, and **solved them manually** before building pipelines for each content type. It can diff C++ files of tens of thousands of lines in **under 100ms** on a 2023 ThinkPad T14s. It’s still in development as v0.3.0, and the author says they’ve used it daily as their Git difftool for months.

cards.camps: Two camps: fans praise its effort and minimal diffs; skeptics question its output, compare it with Delta, or criticize its license and installation options.

comments.text: > can diff 99.95% of code changes I’m not sure if I’m understanding this correctly : so for the remaining 0.05% of code changes, this tool would just… miss it? That seems horrible for a diff tool :O

For me the biggest issue is “git rebase” merge conflicts because the surrounding context was modified (especially near beginning/end of functions where the context includes unrelated stuff), or similar in a markdown document. (If commit A adds a line to the end of a bullet list in markdown and commit B does the same, they will conflict even though resolution is trivial for a human)

glossary.labor share: The portion of a country's economic output that workers receive as wages and salaries.
glossary.GDP: Gross Domestic Product: the total value of what a country's economy produces.
glossary.capital: Things people or companies own and use to make income, like equipment or ownership in a business.
glossary.automation: Using machines or software to do work people used to do.
glossary.jobless growth: When an economy grows but adds few jobs or loses jobs.
glossary.K-shaped economy: An economy where some people's fortunes rise while others' fall.
glossary.AI: Artificial intelligence: computer systems designed to do tasks people associate with thinking.
glossary.HDMI: High-Definition Multimedia Interface: the cable connection that carries picture and sound from one device to a screen.
glossary.Ethernet: A wired way for devices to connect to a network, often using a cable.
glossary.rooting: Getting deeper control of a device than its maker normally allows.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.serialization anomaly: A database mistake where simultaneous changes produce a result that should not be possible.
glossary.foreign key: A database rule that prevents a record from pointing to something that isn't there.
glossary.planner: A part of a database that chooses how to find or change the requested data.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.S&P 493: The article's label for the broader group it compares with the Mag 7.
glossary.profit margin: The part of a company's sales left after paying its costs.
glossary.revenue per worker: A company's revenue divided by how many people work there.
glossary.diff: A view showing what changed between two versions of code.
glossary.Git difftool: A separate program Git opens to show changes between file versions.
glossary.CI pipeline: Continuous Integration pipeline: automated checks that run as code changes, helping catch problems.
glossary.AGPLv3: GNU Affero General Public License version 3: a software license with extra sharing rules when someone offers a modified version over a network.
glossary.three-way diff: A comparison of two edited versions and their shared original, helping show how the edits differ.
glossary.phishing: A scam that tricks someone into entering login details on a fake site.
glossary.enumerate: To list items one by one, often to find out what exists.
glossary.SPF: Sender Policy Framework: a way for a domain to say which mail servers are allowed to send email for it.
glossary.DKIM: DomainKeys Identified Mail: a way for an email to carry proof about who sent it.
glossary.DMARC: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance: rules for checking whether email claiming to come from a domain is genuine.
glossary.SaaS: Software as a Service: software you access over the internet, with the provider running it for you.
glossary.clean-room reimplementation: A way to build a compatible product using public information and new code, rather than copying the original.
glossary.drop-in replacement: A new tool designed to take an old one’s place without users changing how they use it.
glossary.self-hosted: Running a service on a computer you control rather than relying on someone else's.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.SDK: Software Development Kit: tools a company provides so people can make apps for its device.
glossary.deregulate: To remove or loosen rules that govern an industry.
glossary.data-brokers: Businesses that collect information about people and use it to make decisions or provide it to others.
glossary.gig economy: Work arranged as individual jobs, often through apps, rather than as a regular job.
glossary.dynamic pricing: Prices that change depending on the situation, such as demand or where a ride is going.
glossary.regulatory capture: When rules meant to control an industry end up helping the companies they are supposed to oversee.
glossary.agent swarm: A group of software agents working on tasks together.
glossary.Mineflayer: A tool named in the article for scripting Minecraft agents.
glossary.PvP: Player versus player: a game mode where players or teams fight one another.
glossary.RTS: Real-Time Strategy: a game where players build forces and make moves continuously rather than taking turns.
glossary.harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
glossary.WICOP: Wafer Integrated Chip on PCB: an LED setup that gets rid of the separate package around the chip.
glossary.micro-LED: A very small LED chip; this article refers to chips under 100µm as micro-LEDs.
glossary.gallium nitride: A material used in LEDs; here, the company says it can make white light from this alone.
glossary.rare-earth materials: A group of materials that white LEDs have used in a layer on a blue LED chip.
glossary.luminous efficacy: How much light a device gives off for the amount of power it uses.
glossary.OOP: Object-oriented programming: a way to organize code into named things that hold information and actions.
glossary.generics: A way to make one piece of code work with different kinds of values.
glossary.low-level: A language that gives the programmer more direct control over how a computer does its work.
glossary.pass by reference: A function gets access to the original value, so changes can affect the one the caller has.
glossary.GC: Garbage collection: a program's automatic cleanup of memory it no longer needs.
glossary.ABI: Application Binary Interface: the agreed rules software uses to communicate with other software.
glossary.FFI: Foreign Function Interface: a way for code in one language to call code written in another.
glossary.pentest: A security check where someone tries to find holes in software before it goes live.
glossary.astroturfing: Paid promotion made to look like regular people's honest opinions.
glossary.B2B: Business-to-business: selling products or services to other companies, rather than individual people.
glossary.UX: User experience: how using a product feels and how easy it is to get things done.
